assessmentSummary.identity: A static single-leg stance that maintains heel, first-metatarsal-head, and fifth-metatarsal-head contact with controlled knee, pelvis, trunk, and a declared support and visual condition.
currentCardFindings: Single-Leg Balance Hold — Tripod Foot and Single-Leg Tripod Balance are the same identity.
Supported eyes-open, unsupported eyes-open, and unsupported eyes-closed are exact variants.
Four links have healthy oEmbed metadata only and remain unviewed candidate media.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Stand on one leg beside an available support when required. Maintain contact through the heel, first-metatarsal head, and fifth-metatarsal head without clawing the toes; keep the stance knee softly flexed and tracking, pelvis and ribs stacked, and head quiet for the declared visual condition and hold time. Touch support or set the lifted foot down before an uncontrolled step, alignment change, breath holding, or symptom.

population.medicalScope: The card is not a diagnostic balance test and does not clear fall risk, injury, or neurologic symptoms.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: The defining action is a static single-leg stance with declared tripod contact and controlled posture.
Naming order does not create another exercise identity.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Declare side, hand support, visual condition, footwear, surface, stance posture, hold duration, touch-down rule, and fall space.
Reaching, unstable surfaces, external load, and perturbation require separate review.

evidence.sourceTitle: How to Evaluate and Improve Foot Strength in Athletes: An Update
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: Foot and ankle musculature contributes to pressure control while knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk musculature organizes posture.
The card does not claim that one muscle or visible arch shape alone determines balance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Single-leg postural control uses ankle, hip, and safe touch-down strategies under the declared sensory condition.
Removing support or vision raises balance complexity without adding external impact.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Complexity rises when hand support and then visual input are removed; physical demand changes more modestly.
Overall exercise difficulty is the maximum of complexity and physical demand.

evidence.sourceTitle: How to Evaluate and Improve Foot Strength in Athletes: An Update
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: Loading is bodyweight through one stance limb; external load and unstable surfaces are excluded.
Track foot, calf, hip, and postural fatigue plus touch-downs, toe clawing, alignment change, and unsafe sway.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Use a firm nonslip surface, clear fall space, adequate light, declared footwear, and stable support when needed.
Eyes-closed work requires close supervision and is not an automatic progression.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Single-leg balance benefits have occurred across varied protocols, so the card uses submaximal quality holds rather than claiming one universal dose.
Actual clean time ends at the first failed posture or safety criterion.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Set the tripod, shift to one leg, soften the knee, stack pelvis and ribs, use the declared visual condition, and hold only while controlled.
Instruction includes the safe support or touch-down strategy.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Stop for pain, giving way, numbness, tingling, dizziness, unsafe sway, unavailable support, or an uncontrolled step.
Restore support or a lower-demand stance before repeating.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Supported, unsupported eyes-open, and eyes-closed holds serve different balance and supervision contexts.
Balance gains are task-sensitive, so universal transfer is not claimed.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Athlete guidance distinguishes expected small sway from symptoms and explains support, touch-down, and nonvideo options.
The athlete reports touch-downs and side differences.

evidence.sourceTitle: How to Evaluate and Improve Foot Strength in Athletes: An Update
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: The coach verifies exact support and sensory conditions and observes foot, knee, pelvis, trunk, breathing, and fall strategy.
Record actual clean hold time and touch-downs rather than only the target.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Stable support, eyes open, shorter holds, secure footwear, touch-down permission, and tandem stance can improve access.
Removing support or vision is optional and requires the exact safety contract.

evidence.sourceTitle: Single Leg Balance Training: A Systematic Review
claims: Supported, unsupported, and eyes-closed conditions are exact variants; footwear and duration are modifiers.
Reach tasks, loaded holds, perturbations, and unstable surfaces require separate definitions.
